listenings.text: People ask me how much of the industry press I read, and the honest answer is almost none of it, which sounds like a confession and is actually the method. Forty pages a week get published about cross-border payments alone. Nobody with a job reads forty pages. What I do takes ten minutes and it is always the same ten minutes. I skim through the summary and the subheadings, fast, and I am not trying to understand anything yet. I am waiting for one thing to snag. Something that contradicts what I thought last month, or a number that is bigger than it should be. When something snags, I stop skimming and I zoom in on that one paragraph and read it properly, twice. Nine of my ten minutes go on two paragraphs. Everything else I have skimmed through and forgotten on purpose, and I have never once regretted it.

Here is something I wish somebody had told me in my first year, because it took me about three years to work out on my own. A press release is not information. It is an argument, written by the company it is about, and paid for by the same company. So it will point out every number that helps it and it will stay completely silent about the one that does not, and none of that is lying. It is selection. The useful question is therefore never is this true. The useful question is what is missing. If a release gives you growth in percentage terms and never once gives you the absolute figure, the absolute figure is small. If it announces a partnership and does not say what either side has committed to, nobody has committed to anything yet. Read what is there, then make a short list of what a normal person would have mentioned and did not appear. That list is the real story.

The thing nobody tells you about keeping up with an industry is that it is a habit and not an event. I have watched very intelligent people try to do it the other way, which is to save everything for a quiet afternoon that never arrives, and then panic-read four hundred pages the night before a conference. That does not work, and it does not work for a reason. What you need is not the information. You already have most of the information. What you need is the pattern, and a pattern is only visible if you look at the same thing at regular intervals. So mine is fifteen minutes on Monday morning, before anything else, every single week. Same three sources, same coffee. Some Mondays there is nothing. But four or five times a year I come across something in those fifteen minutes that changes what my team does that quarter, and none of those things were ever sent to me by anybody.

to mention a subject briefly and then move on
to make sure the reader notices a particular fact

to stop on one small part and read or look at it properly
to notice something that nobody said directly
to present a plan or an argument in an organized order

reading.rtitle: Ten Minutes with a Sector Report
paras: Almost nobody in this industry reads. That sounds like an insult and it is not meant as one: roughly forty pages of sector report, press release and comment are published every week about cross-border payments alone, and a person with an actual job cannot read forty pages. What experienced people do instead is a different skill, and nobody ever teaches it.

It starts with knowing what each kind of page is trying to do. A sector report lays out its whole argument in the executive summary on page two, and the other thirty pages exist to defend it. A press release is written by the company it is about, so it points out every number that helps and stays quiet about the one that does not — which is not lying, it is selection. An opinion piece is one person's argument with a byline on it, and the byline is the most useful line on the page: you read the same sentence differently once you know who pays the author.

So the first move is not to read. The first move is to skim through the summary and the subheadings until something snags — a number that is larger than it should be, a claim that contradicts what you believed last month — and only then to zoom in on that one paragraph and read it twice. A good reader of industry writing spends nine of the ten minutes on two paragraphs. Everything else has been skimmed through and forgotten on purpose.

The second half of the skill is what you do with the paragraph you stopped on. You break the claim down into the two or three things it actually says, because a sentence like "real-time settlement across eleven corridors" is three claims wearing one coat. Then you pick up on what the page avoids. A report that touches on regulation in a single sentence and spends nine pages on technology has told you something about its author that the author did not intend to tell you.

And then there is the part that has nothing to do with any single article. Keeping up with an industry is a habit, not an event: fifteen minutes on a Monday morning, the same three sources, every week, including the Mondays when there is nothing. People who do this come across the useful thing four or five times a year, and the useful thing is never the item that somebody forwarded to them. To sum up: skim, stop once, break it down, and do it on Monday.
